claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9111 §1: 'A cache stores cacheable responses to reduce the response time and network bandwidth consumption on future equivalent requests.' §4.2: 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server'.

RFC 9111 §1: 'A "shared cache" is a cache that stores responses for reuse by more than one user; shared caches are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary. A "private cache", in contrast, is dedicated to a single user; often, they are deployed as a component of a user agent.'

RFC 9111 §2: 'Most commonly, caches store the successful result of a retrieval request: i.e., a 200 (OK) response to a GET request ... responses to methods other than GET if the method's definition allows such caching'. RFC 9110 §9.3.3: 'a POST request cannot be satisfied by a cached POST response because POST is potentially unsafe'. Lesson says 'normally'.

RFC 9111 §5.2.2.1: 'The max-age response directive indicates that the response is to be considered stale after its age is greater than the specified number of seconds.' §4.2: 'A response's "age" is the time that has passed since it was generated by, or successfully validated with, the origin server.'

RFC 9111 §4.2.4: 'A cache MUST NOT generate a stale response unless it is disconnected or doing so is explicitly permitted by the client or origin server'. §1: a stale response 'might still be reusable if validation can freshen it'. Lesson hedges with 'barring exceptions'.

RFC 9110 §8.8.3: 'The "ETag" field in a response provides the current entity tag for the selected representation ... An entity tag is an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource'.

RFC 9111 §4.3.1: a cache 'MUST send the relevant entity tags (using If-Match, If-None-Match, or If-Range) if the entity tags were provided in the stored response'. RFC 9110 §13.1.2: If-None-Match is evaluated against the selected representation's current entity tag.

RFC 9111 §4.3.3: 304 'indicates that the stored response can be updated and reused'; for a full response 'the cache MUST use the full response to satisfy the request. The cache MAY store such a full response'. RFC 9110 §15.4.5: a 304 'cannot contain content or trailers.'

RFC 9110 §15.4.5 (under §15.4 Redirection 3xx): 'the server is therefore redirecting the client to make use of that stored representation as if it were the content of a 200 (OK) response.' and a 304 'cannot contain content or trailers.'

RFC 9111 §4.2.2: 'a cache MAY assign a heuristic expiration time when an explicit time is not specified, employing algorithms that use other field values (such as the Last-Modified time)'. Lesson: 'each cache falls back to its own rules and they may disagree'.

RFC 9111 §4.2: 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server, thereby improving efficiency.' A copy reused without contacting the origin cannot reflect a change made there meanwhile.

RFC 9111 §4.2: 'When a response is fresh, it can be used to satisfy subsequent requests without contacting the origin server'. §1: shared caches 'are usually (but not always) deployed as a part of an intermediary'.

cache-headers.sh@stage-0: each step is a separate curl with -o /dev/null, no cache option. RFC 9111 §4.2 is permissive ('can be used ... without contacting the origin server'); nothing obliges reuse of a fresh copy. Live: the same GET without If-None-Match reached the origin and got 200.

First half verified: RFC 9111 §5.2.1.4 'The no-cache request directive indicates that the client prefers a stored response not be used to satisfy the request without successful validation on the origin server.' Second half (a browser refresh can send such a request) is browser behaviour; RFC 9111 §4.2 only says freshness 'cannot be used to force a user agent to refresh its display or reload a resource'. No browser docs in versions.yaml. Kind behavior; lesson hedges with 'can'.

issues.text: Round-1 minor not applied. Keyed option a still carries a false absolute: an Etag is not 'only ever' compared against the origin's version. RFC 9111 §4.3.2: a cache receiving a conditional request 'SHOULD evaluate any applicable conditional header field preconditions ... with respect to the corresponding validators contained within the stored response.' Key remains the only correct option (b, c, d plainly wrong).
issues.quote: the `Etag` is only ever compared for equality against the version the origin holds
issues.fix: Option a (en): '`max-age=60` is a count of seconds the copy may still be served on its own; the `Etag` is compared for equality to tell whether a held copy is still the current version'. vi: bỏ 'chỉ dùng để', thay bằng 'được so bằng để biết bản đang giữ có còn là phiên bản hiện tại'.

issues.text: "Barring exceptions" tells me a cache sometimes does not ask first with a stale copy, but the lesson never says what those exceptions are or that they are out of scope. Not needed for the main idea; I stopped to wonder.
issues.quote: Stale does not mean deleted; barring exceptions, the cache asks first, so it revalidates
issues.fix: Drop "barring exceptions" or replace it with "apart from rare cases this lesson leaves out".

issues.text: Re-read twice. "because the cache sent If-None-Match" reads as the reason the 304 stays between cache and origin, but the point just made is that the cache turns the 304 into a 200 for the client.
issues.quote: the `304` travels only between cache and origin, because the cache sent `If-None-Match`.
issues.fix: Rephrase as: "the `304` never reaches the client: it answers the cache's `If-None-Match`, and only the cache holds the copy it refers to."

issues.text: "serves files from disk as they are and a few fixed paths" parses oddly: I read "serves ... a few fixed paths" only on the second pass, and I cannot tell how a fixed path differs from a file.
issues.quote: Caddy, the lab's web server, serves files from disk as they are and a few fixed paths, one written for this lesson.
issues.fix: Split: "Caddy, the lab's web server, serves files from disk as they are. A few paths get special rules; one was written for this lesson."

issues.text: "renders" is not in my vocabulary; I guess it means "shows on screen", which is enough to get the point.
